title: Check-for-Understanding & Exit Tickets
subtitle: Short, teacher-owned formative checks that make student thinking visible — so you can act on it, not just collect it.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: NCTM, Principles to Actions (ETP 8, 2014) · Wiliam, Embedded Formative Assessment · connects to My Favorite No & Fluency Practice here.

blocks.text: Quick formative checks — during the lesson (CFU) and at the close (an exit ticket) — designed to **surface how students are thinking**, not just whether they got an answer, so the teacher can respond.

This is NCTM Effective Teaching Practice #8, *elicit and use evidence of student thinking*. The framework names it as a pillar — and the move that closes the loop. A good exit ticket isn’t a grade; it’s a window into misconceptions you’ll act on tomorrow.

This is a *teacher’s* tool for seeing their own students’ thinking, kept separate from leadership measurement. You likely already have exit tickets/CFUs you’ve built — this tool is about using them to **elicit and then USE** the evidence (the “use” is the part most often skipped).

blocks.label: Effective Teaching Practices
items: Elicit & use evidence of student thinking
Establish mathematics goals
Pose purposeful questions

blocks.label: Strands of Mathematical Proficiency
items: Conceptual understanding
Adaptive reasoning

rows: During the lesson, before moving on — a quick read so you don’t build on sand (a problem on whiteboards, a thumbs-and-explain, a turn-and-talk you listen in on).
At the close — 1–2 questions that reveal whether the day’s goal landed and surface misconceptions to act on next.

yes.title: A good check
items: Targets the day’s specific learning goal
Reveals *thinking* (“show your strategy / explain why”)
Is short — 1–2 items, a few minutes
Is designed to expose a likely misconception
Gets *used* — sorted, read, acted on

no.title: A wasted check
items: 10 answer-only items (a mini-quiz, not a window)
Collected and graded but never read for patterns
Unconnected to the lesson goal
So long it eats the close
Used only as a compliance/points grab

blocks.text: The most common failure isn’t a bad exit ticket — it’s a fine one that’s collected and never acted on. If the evidence doesn’t change *something* (tomorrow’s opener, a small-group, the next launch), the loop never closed. The value is in the using.

items: **Checks that reveal thinking** catch a struggling student’s misconception early, before it compounds into a failing unit test.
**“Explain your reasoning” prompts** — with sentence stems — give MLLs a structured way to show understanding that a multiple-choice item hides.
**Keep them low-stakes** (not heavily graded) so students show their real thinking instead of guessing what the teacher wants.

blocks.text: Where it lives in the lesson

CFUs run **throughout** (before you move on); the exit ticket runs at the **close**. Both belong to Practice & Closure, and both exist to inform what you do next — in the moment, tomorrow, or in a small group.
Using the evidence (the part that matters)

rows: A quick check says “most aren’t there yet” → pause, address it now, before building further.
Sort the tickets into a few piles (got it / partial / common misconception). The biggest misconception pile becomes tomorrow’s launch or opener.
The “partial” pile tells you exactly who to pull while others start independent work.

blocks.text: Don’t grade them — **sort into 3 piles** (got it / almost / not yet + the common error). Ninety seconds of sorting tells you more about tomorrow’s lesson than a graded score ever will, and it surfaces the exact wrong answer to use.

items: **One or two items, tied to today’s goal** — resist the mini-quiz.
**Ask for thinking:** “Solve *and* explain your strategy,” or “Which is correct and why?”
**Include an item that exposes the likely misconception** — you want to *see* the error, not avoid it.
**Keep it low-stakes** so students show real thinking, not a guess at what you want.

blocks.title: It closes the loop with the openers

blocks.text: This is the connective tissue between Practice & Closure and the next day’s Opener: **today’s exit ticket becomes tomorrow’s *My Favorite No* or Number Talk.** The misconception you spot at 2:45 is the perfect, authentic opener at 8:05. Elicit at the close, use at the open.

items: **Whiteboards:** all students solve one problem, hold up — you scan the room.
**Thumbs + explain:** not just thumbs-up, but “tell your partner why.”
**Listen in on a turn-and-talk** — the lowest-effort CFU there is.
**Hinge question:** one well-chosen question whose answer tells you whether to move on or reteach.
**Use the evidence to act early** — catching a misconception at the close is how you keep a struggling student from falling further behind by the test.
**Offer “explain in words/picture/numbers”** so MLLs and diverse thinkers can show understanding in more than one way.
**Keep it ungraded/low-stakes** so the ticket measures thinking, not test-taking nerves.

blocks.text: A simple, used formative loop is what makes the whole framework self-correcting: you see what students actually understand, and you adjust the next opener, task, or small group accordingly. It’s the quiet engine that keeps instruction responsive — and it runs on tools you already have.
